you." "Leave me? No, no, Jane. I only ask you to endure one more night under this roof, and then we will go to a villa I have in the south of France. You shall be my wife as if I were not married."
I shook my head. "If I lived with you like that, I would be your mistress."
"What a fool I am!" Mr. Rochester cried. "I keep saying that I'm not married, but I forget that you know nothing of that infernal woman or the circumstances of our union."
He began by telling me what I'd already heard from Mrs. Fairfax—that his father didn't want him to be poor when Rowland, his older brother, inherited everything.
Then Rochester said that his father and Rowland arranged for him to marry Bertha Mason, who had a dowry of thirty thousand pounds.
He went to Jamaica and was dazzled by the beautiful Bertha. "I seldom saw her alone, but every man seemed to admire her and envy me.
A marriage took place almost before I knew where I was. I never loved her. I didn't even know her!"
He thought his wife's mother was dead. Only after the wedding did he learn that she was shut up in an insane asylum, as was Bertha's younger brother.
"My father and Rowland knew all this but thought only of Bertha's dowry. I lived with her for four years.

I will spare you the abominable details except to say that no servant would stay because of the continued outbreaks of her violent temper, and I couldn't divorce her because the doctors had discovered that she was insane."
"I sincerely pity you, sir," I said quietly. "Go on."
One night in Jamaica, Mr. Rochester decided to flee to Europe, where he could live without anyone knowing his past.
He brought Bertha back to Thornfield and left her in the care of Grace Poole.
For ten years he roamed from one country to another. He had three mistresses, including Adele's mother, Celine Varens.
"I now hate to remember the time I spent with those women," he said.
I felt the truth of those words and knew if I became his next mistress, he would one day regard me the same way.
"I was searching for love," he said, "but never found it until one day when I was returning to Thornfield on business. My horse slipped on some ice—"
"Don't talk to me of those days, sir," I interrupted, wiping tears from my eyes.
"All I ask, Jane, is that you promise to be mine."
"Mr. Rochester, I will not be yours." I rose from my chair.
"Oh, Jane! My hope, my love, my life!" He cried out in anguish and a sob escaped his lips.
I kissed his cheek and fled the room.
The next morning I slipped quietly from Thornfield.
I carried a small parcel containing only some clothing, a locket, and a ring. My purse held twenty shillings.
I was weeping wildly as I walked along my solitary way. At any moment I could have turned back and been welcomed by my master, but I pressed on.
When I heard a coach approaching, I turned and signaled it to stop.
I asked the driver where he was going, and he named a faraway place where I was sure Mr. Rochester had no connections.
The fare would cost every shilling I had, but I climbed aboard, and the coach rolled away.
Two days passed, and the coachman could take me no farther for the sum I had given him.
He set me down at Whitcross, which was not a town but merely a crossroads with a sign showing the distances to four towns. The nearest town was ten miles away.
Suddenly I realized that I'd left my parcel, containing my clothing and jewelry, on the coach.
I was absolutely alone and destitute in the midst of the moors. Evening was coming. What was I going to do?
I feared that a traveler might pass and wonder why I lingered at the signpost, so I left the road and waded into the dark heath.
I found shelter for the night under a moss-covered granite crag. I might have passed a peaceful night, but my heart was broken.
The next morning I returned to Whitcross and from there followed a road until I heard a church bell.
About two o'clock I entered a village, where I immediately noticed a shop with some rolls in the window.
With a roll, I could regain a degree of energy; without one, it would be difficult to go on. What did I have to trade?
Only a small silk handkerchief tied at my throat and my gloves. I entered the shop.
"May I help you?" inquired the woman at the counter.
I was seized with shame and couldn't make my request. "I'm tired. May I sit for a moment?"
Looking disappointed, she pointed to a seat, and I sank into it. I wanted to weep but restrained myself. I decided to inquire about employment.
"Are there any dressmakers in the village?" I asked.
"Two or three. That's all we need."
"Do you know of anyplace where a servant is wanted?"
"No, I don't think so."
I asked her what most people did here, and she said they either worked on the farms or at the foundry or in Mr. Oliver's needle factory. But Mr. Oliver didn't employ women.
"What do the women do?" I asked.
"I have no idea. Poor people must get by as they can."
A customer came in, and I left. For most of the afternoon I walked through the village.
I approached houses and then wandered away, realizing I had no right to ask for help. But then I remembered the church.
People who arrive at a place without friends sometimes apply to the minister for introductions.
At the parsonage an old woman answered the door.
"Is the minister in?" I asked.
"No, his father died suddenly. He's three miles away at Moor House and will likely stay two more weeks."
"Is there a lady of the house?"
The woman shook her head and said that the minister wasn't married and she was only a servant.
I was not yet ready to beg so I stumbled away, but I kept thinking of those rolls in the village shop.
I found the shop again, and removing my handkerchief, I went in.
"Would you give me a roll for this handkerchief?"
The woman looked at me with suspicion. "No, I never sell things that way."
Almost desperate, I asked for half a roll, and she again refused.
"How do I know where you got that handkerchief?" she demanded.
"Would you take my gloves?"
"No!" she cried. "What would I do with those?"
Reader, it's not pleasant to dwell on these details. Let me just say that I begged some bread from a farmer that evening and spent the night in the woods.
Toward morning it rained, and the whole next day was wet. I ate only once, when I begged a girl for the cold porridge she was about to throw into a pig trough.
I sought work all day but found nothing. By nightfall I had strayed far from the village, but in the blackness, a small point of light sprang up.
Something about the light pulled me toward it through the rain.
After crossing a marsh, I came to a long, low house. I peered through a window and saw the candle that had been my beacon burning on a table.
An elderly woman was knitting, and two young women, dressed in mourning clothes, sat near the hearth.
The girls appeared to be consulting a dictionary while they read aloud.
As I watched them, I learned that their names were Mary and Diana and that they were studying German.
The housekeeper was named Hannah, and they were all waiting for the return of the girls' brother, St. John.
I was so absorbed in their conversation that I forgot my own wants until Hannah began to prepare dinner.
I knocked on the door, and Hannah opened it.
"What do you want?" She surveyed me by the light of a candle.
"A night's shelter in a shed or barn and a morsel of bread."
Distrust, the very feeling I dreaded, appeared on Hannah's face. "I'll give you some bread, but we can't take in a vagrant."
"But where shall I go if you drive me away? Oh, please let me speak to your mistresses!" I implored her.
"I don't know what you're doing here, but if anyone's with you—burglars and the like—tell them we're not alone. We have a gentleman and dogs and guns."
She slammed the door and bolted it.
"But I'll die if you turn me away," I said weakly.
"Everyone must die, but this is not your time," said a nearby voice.
"Who's there?" I cried in terror.
A man went up to the door and knocked.
Hannah opened the door. "Oh, Mr. St. John!
Your sisters have been so worried, and there are bad folks about. A beggar woman—why there she is! Move along!"
"Hush, Hannah," he said.
"You've done your duty in excluding her. Now let me do mine in admitting her."
Soon I stood before the hearth that I had seen through the window. St. John bade me sit down while his sisters fetched bread and milk.
"Try to eat," Diana said as she gently fed me.
Mary removed my wet bonnet. "What's your name?"
"Jane Elliott." I had earlier decided to assume an alias to avoid detection.
"What account can you give of yourself?" said St. John.
"Please, sir, spare me from conversation tonight. My breath is short, and I feel a spasm when I speak."
All three silently surveyed me. "Let's go into the parlor and talk this over," St. John said to his sisters.
A few minutes later Diana returned with instructions for Hannah, who escorted me upstairs to a warm, dry bed.
My memories of the next three days and nights are very dim, but I know that Diana and Mary appeared at my bedside once or twice a day.
"It's good we took her in," whispered Mary during one visit. "She certainly would have died if she stayed outside all night. I wonder what she has suffered."
"Strange hardships, I imagine," said Diana. "She seems like an educated person from her manner of speaking, and her clothes are fine and barely worn."
On the afternoon of the fourth day, I struggled from bed, washed and dressed myself with difficulty, and went down to the kitchen, where Hannah was busy baking.
The young ladies and their brother had gone for a walk, but would soon be back for tea.
As I watched Hannah make a pie, she told me about the Rivers family and their home, which was known as Moor House.
St. John Rivers was a minister at a church a few miles away in Morton, the very place where I'd tried to trade my things for a roll.
His sisters worked as governesses in a distant city and had come home for their father's recent funeral.
"You're up!" cried Mary when the three siblings returned. "You still look so pale and thin, poor girl."
"What are you doing in the kitchen?" asked Diana. "Mary and I like to sit here, but you're a visitor and must go into the parlor."
She assisted me into the parlor, where I sat on a sofa to wait for tea.
St. John sat opposite me, silently reading, so I used the time to study him.
He was in his late twenties, tall and slender, with a classically handsome face and fair hair.
When tea was placed on the table, St. John addressed me for the first time, urging me to eat slowly so as not to make myself ill.
"I hope I won't be eating long at your expense, sir," I replied.
"No," he said coolly. "When you've given us the address of your friends, we'll see that you're returned home."
"I must tell you that I have no family or friends."
All three looked at me, but I felt no suspicion in their eyes, only curiosity.
"You've never been married?" St. John glanced at my hands, looking for a wedding ring.
Diana laughed. "She can't be more than 17 or 18 years old, St. John."
"I'm almost 19, and no, I'm not married."
I felt my face grow hot as bitter memories were awakened by the mention of marriage. They all saw the embarrassment and the emotion in my face.
Diana and Mary looked away, but their colder and sterner brother continued to stare until tears filled my eyes.
"Where did you last live?" he asked.
"You are too inquisitive, St. John," murmured Mary, but he leaned over the table and required an answer with a second firm and piercing look.
"Where I lived and with whom are my secrets," I replied concisely.
"And, in my opinion, you have the right to keep those secrets from St. John and every other questioner," said Diana.
"But if I know nothing about you, I can't help you," St. John said to me. "And you need help, don't you?"
"I do." I had now drunk my tea and was quite refreshed. "I will tell you as much of my story as I can without compromising my own peace of mind and security and that of others." And
so I told them that I was an orphan, educated at Lowood, and that until recently I was a governess. It
was too dangerous to explain the reason for my departure, but I was blameless. "Don't
make her talk anymore now, St. John," said Diana when I paused. "Miss Elliott is tired." I
startled at the sound of that name, and St. John noticed at once. "You did say your name was Jane Elliott?" "Yes,
I have taken an alias because I fear discovery above all else. I do not want to be dependent on you for long. Show
me how to seek work, then let me go, but until then, allow me to stay here." "Indeed
you shall stay here," Diana said firmly. "You
shall ," repeated Mary.
"I will be a dressmaker or a servant," I vowed.
"If such is your spirit," St. John said without emotion, "I promise to aid you in my own time and way."
He then resumed his reading, and I soon went to bed.
As the days passed, I found that the more I knew Diana and Mary, the more I liked them.
They were better educated than I was, and Diana offered to teach me German.
When they discovered I could draw, they gave me their pencils and watercolors.
I did not feel such a connection to St. John, but that may have been because he was often away, tending to his parishioners. He also had a reserved, brooding nature.
A month sped by, and Diana and Mary were soon to leave Moor House.
St. John was going back to the parsonage, but he'd said nothing to me about the employment he had promised, so one morning I ventured to inquire.
"Two years ago Morton had no school," he replied. "I started one for boys, and now I'm opening one for girls.
I fear the work is beneath you, but would you be the schoolmistress?"
"Thank you, Mr. Rivers," I said quickly. "I accept your offer."
"You do understand that it's only a village school? Knitting, sewing, reading, writing, and mathematics will be all you'll teach."
I understood and told him I was still happy to accept the position.
Diana and Mary became sadder and more silent as the day approached for their departure.
They hinted that they might never see St. John again because he intended to become a missionary.
Adding to their gloom was a newly arrived letter announcing that their uncle John had died.
Years before, John had given their father some bad financial advice that had ruined the elder Mr. Rivers.
They had always hoped that John would atone for this by leaving them his estate, but the letter said that he had bequeathed twenty thousand pounds to another relative.
The next day I left Moor House for Morton. Diana and Mary soon returned home, and with St. John and Hannah leaving a week later, the old house was abandoned.
My new home was a cottage, furnished simply by Rosamond Oliver, the only daughter of the richest man in the valley.
On the first day of school, I had twenty pupils. Only three could read; none could write or do a simple sum.
I felt degraded by my position and dismayed at the ignorance and poverty around me, but I hoped my attitude would improve as my students progressed.
That evening I stood at my cottage door and asked myself one question.
Which was better: to have surrendered to temptation and live in France as Mr. Rochester's mistress, or to be a schoolmistress, free and honest, in an English village?
As I surveyed the quiet fields before my cottage, I knew I'd made the right choice, but still I wept.
Mr. Rochester had loved me, and no one would ever love me like that again.
I heard a noise and looked up to see St. John and his dog, Carlo, at my gate.
"I've brought you a parcel that my sisters left for you," he announced as he approached.
"I think it contains watercolors, pencils, and paper."
"Oh, what a welcome gift!" I burst out.
He studied my face, where I know the traces of tears remained. "Have you found your first day's work harder than you expected?" he asked.
"On the contrary, I think in time I shall enjoy my pupils."
"A year ago I was miserable because I thought I'd made a mistake in entering the ministry," he confided.
"I longed for a more active life, but now I know that God has a purpose for me: I've resolved to be a missionary."
Carlo barked, and I saw a beautiful young woman, dressed all in white, coming toward us. St. John stared at her but said nothing.
"Good evening, Mr. Rivers," said the woman. "Your dog is friendlier than you are. If he could speak, he wouldn't be silent."
St. John flushed; he looked at the ground and crushed some flower buds underneath his foot.
"Did I furnish your cottage nicely?" she asked me.
"Very nicely indeed." I realized that this beauty was Rosamond Oliver.
She turned her attention to St. John again. "Papa is alone this evening and not well. Won't you return with me and visit him?"
"Not tonight, Miss Rosamond. It's too late for a visit."
St. John spoke mechanically. But I could hear in his low, hollow voice how painful it was for him to refuse her.
"Well, then I shall be going," she said to him. "I'll visit the schoolroom," she promised me.
As the months passed, my pupils began to make progress, and I felt that I was becoming a favorite in the neighborhood.
At this point I was happy more often than not, and yet in the midst of this calm, I kept dreaming of Mr. Rochester.
I would awake in the middle of the night, realize where I was, and be filled with despair.
But every morning I calmly opened the school and greeted my pupils.
Miss Oliver kept her word about coming to the school. She generally made her visit in the course of her morning ride.
In her purple riding habit and black velvet cap, she would enter the rustic building and glide through the dazzled ranks of the village children.
She often arrived when St. John was giving his daily Bible lesson.
As she gave him a smile, his hands would tremble and his cheeks would burn, but he didn't return her smile.
Miss Oliver also honored me with frequent visits to my cottage.
Indulged from birth, she was very different from St. John's sisters. Still, I liked her almost as much as I liked Adele.
One evening while rummaging through my cupboard, she discovered my drawing materials and some sketches.
"Would you make a portrait of me for Papa?" she asked.
"With pleasure."
I was thrilled at the idea of capturing such a perfect subject. I took a sheet of fine cardboard and drew a careful outline.
As it was late in the day, I promised myself the pleasure of coloring the picture another time.
A few days later it was a holiday, so I devoted that November afternoon to completing the portrait.
I was absorbed in the finishing touches when, after one quick knock, St. John entered my cottage.
"I've brought you a new book of poetry." He handed me the book.
While I eagerly glanced at the poetry, St. John stooped to examine my drawing, but startled by its subject, he immediately stood upright.
"Is this portrait a good resemblance?" I asked bluntly.
"A well-executed picture," he responded. "Very graceful and correct drawing."
"But what of the resemblance? Who does it look like?"
After some hesitation, he said, "Miss Oliver, I presume."
"I'll paint a copy for you, if you like. Would it comfort you or torment you to have such a painting with you when you're a missionary?"
He glanced at me and then at the picture. "I would certainly like to have it, but whether that would be wise is another question."
"She likes you, I'm sure," I said. "You ought to marry her."
"Does she like me?" He seemed startled.
"Certainly. She talks of you constantly; there's no subject she enjoys so much or touches upon so often."
"It's strange," he said, "that while I love her wildly, I know that she's not the partner for me. Rosamond a missionary's wife? Never!"
"But you don't have to be a missionary. You could relinquish that scheme."
"Relinquish my vocation? My work is dearer to me than my own blood."
After a considerable pause, I said, "But what about Miss Oliver? Are her disappointment and sorrow of no interest to you?"
"Miss Oliver is always surrounded by suitors. In less than a month, she'll forget me and marry someone else."
"You speak coolly enough, but you tremble and flush whenever she enters the schoolroom."
"And you are quite bold and original."
He picked up his hat, which lay on the table beside my palette. Once more he looked at the picture.
"She is lovely," he murmured.
"So may I paint a copy for you?"
"No."
He was about to cover the portrait with the thin sheet of paper that I used to keep it clean when he suddenly spotted something. He shot a glance at me.
"What's the matter?" I asked.
"Nothing." But as he replaced the paper, I saw him tear a narrow piece from the edge. It disappeared into his glove, and with a hasty nod and a quick good-bye, he vanished.
I studied the paper, but could see nothing except a few paint stains, so I soon forgot his strange behavior.
When St. John Rivers left my cottage, it was beginning to snow. The whirling storm continued all night and the next day.
By twilight the valley was full of drifts and nearly impassable. For almost an hour, I sat by my hearth listening to the fury of the storm.
At last I lit a candle and began to read my new book of poetry. I heard a noise and supposed it must be the wind shaking the door.
But it was St. John, who came in from the howling darkness and stood before me, his cloak as white as a glacier.
"What has happened?" I demanded. "Is there bad news?"
"No. How easily alarmed you are." He hung up his cloak and stamped the snow from his boots.
Warming his hands at the fire, he said, "I have worked hard to get here. One snowdrift came up to my waist."
"But why are you here?"
"That's a rather inhospitable question to ask a visitor, but since you ask, I'll say simply to have a little talk with you." He sat down.
"I grew tired of my silent books and empty rooms. Besides, since yesterday I've heard half a story, and I'm impatient to hear the rest of it."
I recalled his strange conduct yesterday and began to wonder if he were losing his mind.
But as he began to tell his story, he seemed too calm to be insane.
"Twenty years ago," he said, "a poor clergyman—never mind his name right now—fell in love with a rich man's daughter.
She married him against the advice of all her friends and family, who consequently disowned her right after the wedding.
Within two years they were dead, and their infant daughter was sent to live with an aunt and uncle named Reed of Gateshead."
I started in surprise.
"What's wrong? Did you hear something?" he asked me. "It was probably just a mouse in the walls.
To go on . . . after Mr. Reed died, his wife kept the orphan for ten years and then sent her to Lowood, where you resided for so long.
What strikes me is how many similarities there are between this orphan's story and yours.
She left Lowood to become a governess at the home of a Mr. Rochester."
"Please tell me, Mr. Rivers—"
"I'm almost finished," he interrupted.
"I know nothing of Mr. Rochester's character except that he proposed to this girl, and at the altar, she discovered that he was already married to another woman, who was insane.
Sometime later Mr. Briggs, a London solicitor, needed to contact this governess, but she had fled Thornfield, and no one knew where to find her.
Isn't that the strangest tale?"
"Since you know so much, just tell me this," I said firmly. "Where is Mr. Rochester? What is he doing? Is he well?"
"I know nothing of Mr. Rochester. I only know what Mr. Briggs wrote to me in his letter.
You should ask me the name of the governess and why Mr. Briggs was looking for her."
But I only wanted to hear about Edward Rochester. "Didn't anyone go to Thornfield? Didn't anyone write to Mr. Rochester?"
"Of course they wrote."
"And what did he reply?" I asked impatiently.
"Mr. Briggs said that his letters were answered not by Mr. Rochester but by a Mrs. Fairfax."
I felt cold and dismayed because my worst fears had probably come true.
Mr. Rochester had left England and rushed abroad in reckless desperation. Oh, my poor master! Oh, my poor Edward!
"He must have been a bad man," said St. John.
"You don't know him, so don't judge him," I snapped.
"Very well," St. John said quietly. "Since you won't ask the name of the governess, I'll show it to you in black and white."
From his pocket he produced a shabby slip of paper that I recognized as the one he'd torn from my cover sheet yesterday.
He got up and held the paper close to my eyes. There I saw in my own handwriting the words "Jane Eyre," doubtless the result of some daydreaming.
"Briggs wrote to me of a Jane Eyre. I know a Jane Elliott, though I confess I have my suspicions about you.
Do you admit that Jane Eyre is your name?"
"Yes, yes," I said quickly, "but where is Mr. Briggs? Perhaps he knows more of Mr. Rochester than you do."
"Briggs is in London, but you haven't asked what he wanted with you."
"Well, what did he want?"
"Merely to tell you that your uncle, Mr. John Eyre of Madeira, is dead and that he left you all his property and that you are now rich."
I was stunned. "Me! Rich?"
"Yes, you're an heiress."
I was so surprised that for a few minutes I was silent. Finally I said, "How much am I worth?"
"Twenty thousand pounds."
"Twenty thousand pounds?" This was a new stunner because I'd been thinking I'd inherited perhaps four or five thousand.
The true amount actually took my breath away for a few minutes.
I had never seen St. John laugh, but he was laughing now.
"Well, if you'd committed a murder and been caught, you couldn't look more shocked than you do at this moment."
He put on his cloak and began to leave.
"Wait! Why did Mr. Briggs contact you? Why did he think that you, living in this remote place, could help find me?"
"Oh, the clergy are often appealed to about odd matters." He lifted the latch.
But his answer did not satisfy me, and I demanded to know more.
With some reluctance he told me that his name was St. John Eyre Rivers and that his mother had two brothers, my father and John Eyre of Madeira.
"So you and Diana and Mary are my cousins!" I exclaimed. "Oh, I'm so glad!"
St. John smiled at my excitement. "You looked serious when I told you about your fortune, but now you're excited about something insignificant."
"It may mean nothing to you, who have two sisters, but I had nobody, and now I have three relatives.
I will regard you as my brother, and Diana and Mary as my sisters."
I paced the room because suddenly I had an idea: I would divide my fortune among the four of us, and I would live at Moor House.
"Oh, no!" St. John protested when he heard my plan. "You are acting on impulse."
But I was firm in my resolve. I would repay my rescuers, and we would each have five thousand pounds.
It was nearly Christmas by the time that all the financial arrangements were settled and I was able to resign from the school.
I had told St. John that I would remain as schoolmistress until he could find a replacement.
As I closed up the school for the holidays, I promised the girls that I would come every week and teach them for an hour.
Watching my students file out of the school, St. John said to me, "What are you going to do now?"
"I intend to be as active as I can," I replied. "First I must beg you to let Hannah come with me to Moor House.
Diana and Mary will be home in a week, and I want to have everything in order for their arrival."
St. John looked puzzled. "I don't understand what employment you're proposing for yourself. What is your aim in life now?"
"My first aim will be to clean Moor House from top to bottom; my next will be to polish it until everything gleams; my third will be to arrange every piece of furniture with mathematical precision.
Afterward Hannah and I will spend two days in the kitchen baking." I smiled with satisfaction.
"In short, my aim is to have everything in perfect readiness for Diana and Mary's arrival next Thursday."
St. John smiled but still managed to look dissatisfied.
"That's all very well for the present, but I hope you'll soon look beyond household tasks and sisterly society."
I did not understand him. "I'm prepared to be as content as a queen, and you're trying to make me restless. For what purpose?"
"For the purpose of using the talents that God has given you."
But working alongside Hannah, I was content, and when Thursday came at last, everything was ready. St. John arrived first.
"Are you finished with housemaid's work?" he asked when he found me in the kitchen.
"Come see the results of my labors," I said cheerfully.
With great difficulty I persuaded him to tour the house.
As we wandered upstairs and down, he said that I must have gone to a great deal of trouble to have made so much progress in so little time.
But he didn't express any pleasure in my improvements. His silence disturbed me.
I had replaced some curtains and furniture, and I thought perhaps he was upset by these changes.
"Not at all," he said. "You've been quite respectful of the old house.
I only fear that you've bestowed more thought on it than it deserves."
Then he asked me where a certain book was. I removed it from a shelf, and he withdrew to a window seat to read.
Watching him, I contemplated his lack of pleasure in my improvements to his family home and suddenly realized how trying it would be to be his wife.
Diana and Mary soon arrived, bringing joy to Moor House.
Unlike their brother, they were delighted with the new drapery and fresh carpets, and they generously expressed their gratitude.
I'm afraid that the ensuing week tried St. John's patience.
It was Christmas week, and we did nothing but spend it in a sort of merry domestic dissipation.
St. John did not rebuke us for our high spirits, but he was seldom home.
He had the unsociable habit of reading at meals, and one morning at breakfast, Diana asked him about his plans.
"I'm planning to leave for India in the coming year," he responded.
"And Rosamond Oliver?" asked Mary.
St. John closed his book and said calmly, "Rosamond Oliver is about to be married."
His sisters and I looked at each other and then at him, but his face remained unchanged.
The next time we were alone, I was tempted to ask if Miss Oliver's marriage distressed him, but he seemed to need little sympathy.
As his sisters and I resumed our usual quiet activities, he spent more time with us.
He had promised to treat me as a sister, but he confided in me less often than when I had been merely the village schoolmistress.
One afternoon I was not able to make my usual visit to the village school because I had a cold.
Mary and Diana went in my place. I sat reading German poetry while St. John studied Hindustani, the language he would need as a missionary.
When I looked up for a moment, I saw him staring at me.
"Jane, I want you to give up German and learn Hindustani."
"Why?"
He explained that it would greatly help him to have a pupil with whom he could converse.
For quite some time he had been considering asking me or his sisters, but he had settled on me because I could sit at a task the longest of the three.
He was not a man to be lightly refused, so I consented.
When Diana and Mary returned, they said that he never would have been able to persuade them to take such a step, and he agreed.
As the weeks passed, I began to feel that he was taking over my mind.
I no longer felt that I could talk or laugh freely in front of him because that annoyed him.
I wanted to please him more every day, but I also felt that I had to disown half of myself to do so.
Perhaps, reader, you think that I had forgotten Mr. Rochester amid these changes of place and fortune. Not for a moment.
The craving to know what had become of him followed me everywhere.
When I was the village schoolmistress, I had reentered my cottage every evening wondering about his fate, and now at Moor House, I brooded over it each night in my bedroom.
In the course of my correspondence with Mr. Briggs about my uncle's will, I had inquired if he knew anything about Mr. Rochester's present residence and state of health.
But as St. John had conjectured, Mr. Briggs knew nothing. I then wrote to Mrs. Fairfax, entreating her for information about Mr. Rochester.
I felt sure that my letter would elicit a prompt response.
I was astonished when two weeks passed without a reply.
When two months wore away, and day after day the post arrived and brought me nothing, I fell prey to the keenest anxiety.
I wrote again because there was a chance that my first letter had gone astray.
For a few weeks I was hopeful, but my hope faded when not a word reached me.
After six months wasted in vain expectancy, my hope died out completely, and I felt dark indeed.
Fine spring days blossomed around me, but I could not enjoy them. Diana thought that I looked ill and offered to accompany me to the seaside.
St. John opposed this, saying that I didn't want a vacation.
"You need employment," he said to me. "Your present life is too purposeless."
In part to give me a purpose, he prolonged my Hindustani lessons and grew more urgent in requiring their completion.
Like a fool I never thought of resisting him—because I could not resist him.
One day in May, I came to my lesson in lower spirits than usual. Hannah had told me that there was a letter for me.
I rushed downstairs, hoping for news of Mr. Rochester, but found only a note from Mr. Briggs about some minor matter. I was still crying as I worked on my lesson.
St. John called me to his side to read, and in attempting to do this, my words were lost in sobs.
"We'll wait a few minutes, Jane, until you are more composed."
Having stifled my sobs and muttered something about not feeling well that morning, I completed my task.
"Now, Jane, you shall take a walk with me."
"I'll call Diana and Mary to come with us."
"No. I want only one companion this morning. Put on your things and wait for me outside."
I obeyed him, and soon we were treading the wild path of the valley.
Approaching a spot where the creek became a waterfall, we sat down on some rocks.
After a long silence, St. John announced, "Jane, I leave for India in six weeks.
God's work is my glory and joy. It seems strange to me that others do not burn to join in the same enterprise."
I felt as if some awful spell were gathering over me while he spoke, a spell that would leave me helpless to resist him.
"Jane, come with me to India as my wife and fellow laborer," said St. John.
"You are meant for work, not for love. A missionary's wife you must be."
"But I don't feel that God has called me to that life! I'm not fit for it!"
"Who is fit for this work?" He leaned back against a rock, and I realized he was prepared for a long argument.
"Give me fifteen minutes to think," I implored him.
He agreed and strode a little distance up the path, where he threw himself down on the heath and lay still.
The case before me was very plain. Mr. Rochester was not here, and even if he were, what could he ever be to me?
My business was to live without him and not drag from day to day, waiting for some impossible change in circumstances that might reunite us.
I believed I must accept St. John's proposal, and yet I shuddered. St. John approved of me but would never love me.
I was a hard worker, and he prized me as a soldier valued a good weapon. There was only one way that I could go to India.
When he returned, I announced, "I will go to India with you if I may go as your sister, not your wife."
He shook his head.
"If you were my real sister, it would be different, but how can I, a man not yet thirty, take to India a girl of nineteen who is not my wife?
It is known that you are not my sister. To attempt to introduce you as such would cast suspicion on us both. We must be married."
But I knew we must not be married because we didn't love each other as a husband and wife should. I stood up and faced him.
"I scorn your idea of love," I said.
He stared at me in silence, and I could not tell whether he was angered or surprised.
At last he announced that he was leaving for Cambridge the next day and would be gone for two weeks.
"Take that time to consider my offer," he said, "and if you reject it, remember it is not me you deny but God."
He did not leave for Cambridge the next day, but delayed his departure for a week.
Without one overt act of hostility, he let me know that he would never forget that I had scorned him.
I felt that if I were his wife, he could soon kill me without drawing a drop of blood. And I told him that one day when he once again proposed to me.
"I know to what your heart clings," he said as we stood outside by the gate.
"You still think about Mr. Rochester even though you should have crushed your interest in him long ago."
I admitted this was true with my silence.
"Are you going to look for Mr. Rochester?" he asked.
"I must find out what has become of him."
"I will remember you in my prayers." St. John opened the gate, strayed toward the valley, and was soon out of sight.
On reentering the parlor, I found Diana at the window. "Jane, you look so pale and agitated these days. What's wrong?"
"St. John has asked me to marry him."
Diana clapped her hands. "This is just what Mary and I have hoped for. You will marry him, won't you? And then he'll stay in England."
"His sole interest in proposing to me was to find a fellow laborer for his work in India."
Diana's face fell. "You wouldn't last three months there! Oh, Jane, please tell me you haven't accepted him."
"I have refused him."
We talked until I saw St. John returning from his walk.
I hurried upstairs because I didn't want to see him, but I was forced to meet him again at supper and at evening prayers.
After prayers Diana and Mary bid him good-bye because he was leaving early the next morning for Cambridge.
I gave him my hand and wished him a pleasant journey. In response, he laid his hand on my head and began to pray.
I stood motionless under his touch and suddenly felt that I could marry him if that was God's will.
At that moment I heard a voice cry out. "Jane! Jane! Jane!"
I started. "What's wrong?" asked St. John.
"Oh, where are you?" I called because the voice was that of Edward Fairfax Rochester, speaking in pain and woe.
"I'm coming!" I cried. "Wait for me!" I flew to the door and ran out into the garden, but no one was there.
The next morning I arose at dawn and occupied myself for an hour or two arranging my things in preparation for a brief absence.
I heard St. John leave his room and stop outside my door.
I feared that he would knock, but he merely slipped a note under my door.

Jane—You left me too suddenly last night. If you had stayed only a little longer, you would have chosen the life of a missionary's wife. I'll expect your final decision when I return in two weeks. Meanwhile I will pray for you hourly.—Yours, St. John
Although it was June, the morning was overcast and chilly, with a driving rain. I heard the front door close.
Looking out my window, I saw St. John headed in the direction of Whitcross, where he would meet the coach.
I, too, would be meeting a coach at Whitcross that day.
"Before long I will know something of him whose voice seemed to summon me last night," I said to myself.
"My letters have been fruitless, so I will make inquiries in person."
At breakfast I announced to Diana and Mary that I was going on a journey and would be absent at least four days.
They asked few questions, only wondering if I were well enough to undertake a trip because I looked so pale.
I replied that nothing bothered me except anxiety about a friend and I hoped to alleviate that soon.
At four o'clock that afternoon, I stood at the signpost in Whitcross.
The coach arrived—the same vehicle that had left me here nearly a year ago.
After a journey of thirty-six hours, I arrived at the Rochester Arms, an inn only two miles from Thornfield.
I could have asked someone at the inn about Mr. Rochester, but I dreaded the reply, so I set off for Thornfield on foot.
Perhaps Mr. Rochester would be standing at his window or walking in the orchard. Or perhaps he wasn't even in England anymore.
Passing along the lower wall of the orchard, I cautiously peeked around the great stone pillar of a gate.
Expecting to view the front of the mansion, I was stunned to see a blackened ruin.
No wonder that my letters had received no answer. A fire had obviously destroyed Thornfield, but how had it started?
I hurried back to the inn. When the innkeeper brought my breakfast, I asked him to sit with me.
But I hardly knew where to begin, so worried was I about his potential answers.
"You know Thornfield, of course?" I finally managed to say.
"Yes, I was the late Mr. Rochester's butler."
"The late!" I gasped. "Is he dead?"
"I mean Mr. Edward Rochester's father," he explained, and I breathed again.
"Is Mr. Rochester living at Thornfield now?" I knew the answer to that question but asked it anyway.
"Oh no. You must be a stranger or you'd know that Thornfield burned down last autumn. The fire broke out in the dead of night."
"The dead of night!" That was always the hour for trouble at Thornfield. "Does anyone know how it started?"
The innkeeper edged his chair a little nearer to the table and spoke softly.
"There was an insane woman in the house. No one ever saw her, but there had always been rumors, and it turned out she was Mr. Rochester's wife!
That news was discovered when a young governess—"
I dreaded hearing my own story. "But the fire?"
"I'm coming to that. Mr. Edward fell in love with this young governess. The servants said they never saw anybody so in love as he was. He used to—"
"You can tell me that story later. Was there any suspicion that this insane woman was responsible for the fire?"
"It was quite certain that she set it."
He went on to tell me the story. Mrs. Poole was in charge of the insane wife, but sometimes when Mrs. Poole was fast asleep, Mrs. Rochester roamed the house.
That night she set fire to the bed in the next room and then went downstairs and burned the bed in the governess' room.
"Fortunately the governess had run away a few months before.
Mr. Rochester had sought her as if she were the most precious thing in the world, but he never heard a word about her.
He wanted to be alone after that, so he sent his housekeeper, Mrs. Fairfax, to live with relatives, and he sent his ward, Miss Adele, to school."
"So he was at home when the fire broke out?"
"Yes indeed. He went upstairs to get his wife and make sure that the servants were safe. Then they called out to him that his wife was on the roof.
Mr. Rochester went up there to rescue her, but she jumped to her death."
"How horrible! Were any other lives lost?"
"No, but it might have been better if there had been."
"What do you mean?" I asked.
"Mr. Edward is blind."
I had feared worse—that he was insane—but it still took all my courage to ask what had caused this calamity.
"He wouldn't leave the house until everyone was out. As he came down the great staircase, the house crashed around him.
He lost an eye and a hand, and his other eye was so inflamed that he lost the sight in that one too."
"Where is he?" I cried.
"At Ferndean, a manor house on a farm that he owns about thirty miles from here."
"Do you have a carriage? I will pay twice your usual rate if you can get me to Ferndean by nightfall."
The innkeeper left to make the arrangements, and I was soon on my way to Ferndean.
I walked the last mile on foot and reached the house as daylight faded and a light rain fell.
So dank and green were its decaying walls that it was difficult to distinguish the house from the trees that surrounded it.
Just then the door opened, and a figure stepped outside. Cautiously he went down one step and walked forward a few paces.
He stretched out his hand as if to feel the rain. It was my master, Edward Fairfax Rochester! I watched him as he stood in the rain, now falling fast.
His servant, John, appeared at the door. "You should come in, sir. Will you take my arm?"
"Leave me alone."
Mr. Rochester groped his way back into the house and closed the door. I took a deep breath as I approached the door and knocked.
The door at Ferndean was opened by John's wife, Mary, who'd been the cook at Thornfield. She started as if she'd seen a ghost.
"Is it really you, Miss Eyre, come at this late hour to this lonely place?"
"It is indeed, Mary," I replied. "How are you?"
She led me into the kitchen, where I quickly explained that I knew everything that had happened at Thornfield.
While I removed my bonnet and shawl, I asked if I could stay the night. Just then the parlor bell rang.
"When you enter the parlor," I said, "tell your master that someone wants to speak to him, but don't give my name."
"I don't think he'll see you; he refuses everybody."
When Mary returned, she said, "You're to send in your name and your business."
She then filled a glass with water and placed it on a tray with some candles.
"Is that what he rang for?" I asked.
"Yes, he always has candles brought in even though he's blind."
"Give the tray to me, and I'll take it."
The tray shook in my hands, and water spilled from the glass. My heart pounded as Mary opened the parlor door for me.
The parlor was a gloomy room, with only a low fire burning. Mr. Rochester leaned against the mantel while his dog, Pilot, lay off to the side.
With a yelp Pilot bounded toward me and almost knocked the tray from my hand.
"Lie down," I said softly, setting the tray on a table.
I approached Mr. Rochester with the glass of water, and Pilot followed me, still excited.
"Down, Pilot," I said again. Mr.
Rochester took a sip of water. "Is that you, Mary? "Mary's

Who is this? Answer me now!" he ordered loudly.
"Pilot knows me and so does Mary."
Mr. Rochester shook his head in confusion. "What delusion has come over me? I must be insane."
"No, sir, you're not insane." He groped the air in front of him, and I took his hand in mine.
"These are Jane's fingers! If so, there must be more of her." He pulled me into his arms.
"I'm all here, sir, and so glad to be near you again. I'll never leave you from this day forward."
"Never? But I've often dreamed that you returned, and when I awoke the next morning, you were gone."
"This is not a dream, sir. I'm an independent woman now and have the money to live near you forever."
"What do you mean?"
I explained to him about my uncle's bequest and said that I could afford to build a house nearby so that I could always take care of him.
Of course I hoped that he would want to marry me, but I didn't mention that.
We had supper together in the parlor, and he tried to ask me where I had been living, but I refused to tell him anything until the next day.
"Just tell me one thing," he said as I started up the stairs for the night. "Were there only ladies in the house where you've been?"
I laughed as I ran upstairs because now I would have a way to tease him out of his melancholy.
We spent most of the next morning outside, and I told him about the past year.
I left out much of what happened the first three days because I didn't want to inflict any unnecessary pain.
The little I did say hurt him more than I would have wished.
He said he would have given me half his fortune without demanding so much as a kiss in return.
I then went on to tell him about Moor House and my position as schoolmistress.
"Your cousin St. John," Mr. Rochester said. "I assume he's an older man who took little notice of you?"
"Actually, he's not yet thirty and quite handsome. We spent a lot of time together because he was teaching me Hindustani."
"What use could that be to you?"
"He wanted me to go to India as his wife."
"You must go your own way with the husband you have chosen—this St. John Rivers," Mr. Rochester insisted.
I could see that my plan to make him jealous had succeeded. "But he doesn't love me, and I don't love him. I love you
." He smiled as I clung to his neck. "And I love you, Jane. Will you marry
me?" "Yes,
sir." He kissed me and then said, "It's odd to be so happy now when I felt so desperate just the other
night. I missed you so much that I called out your name, and the strangest thing was that I thought I heard you
reply." Remembering the voice I'd heard, I smiled. Then I took his hand and kissed
it. Reader, I married him. After a quiet wedding ceremony, we returned to Ferndean.
In the kitchen I announced to Mary and John that I had married Mr. Rochester.
Both servants approved of the match, as did Diana and Mary when I wrote to them.
I don't know how St. John reacted to the news because he never answered the letter I sent him.
Six months later he wrote to me without mentioning Mr. Rochester or my marriage.
As for Adele I went to visit her at school. She looked pale and thin, and I realized that the school was too strict for a child of her age.
I took her home with me, intending to be her governess, but soon discovered that my husband needed all my attention.
I found Adele a more suitable school nearby, and she grew to be a pleasing and kind companion.
I have now been married ten years, and no woman has ever been closer to her husband than I am.
Mr. Rochester continued to be blind for the first two years of our marriage, but gradually regained some sight in his eye.
When his first-born child was put into his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his eyes as they once were—large, brilliant, and black.
Diana and Mary are both happily married. Diana's husband is a captain in the navy, and Mary's is a clergyman.
We continue to see them on a regular basis.
As for St. John, he followed his intended path and became a missionary in India, but he never married.
Thus Edward and I are happy, and all the more so because those we love are happy too.
